docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram shows the major components and signal connections for the Team 203 microphone board. The MEMS microphone produces an analog signal that is conditioned by the MCP6004 op amp before being sent to the ADC input of the Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano.

The microcontroller provides the digital I/O connections for the push button, red LED, and the 8-pin ribbon cable connector used to interface with the other team boards. The board uses a 5V 1.5A voltage regulator, with the system powered from the 9V 3A unregulated power supply.

docs.title: Component Selection — Microphone Subsystem
docs.text: EGR 304 | Team 203 | Individual subsystem: Microphone

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The microphone subsystem detects sound for the team's interactive cat-toy project. An analog microphone feeds a signal-conditioning amplifier, which supplies the RA0 ADC input on the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The subsystem uses the team's planned 9 V input and regulated 5 V supply. Components were evaluated for analog interface compatibility, power consumption, PCB integration, cost, and audio performance. The microphone needs a separate lower-voltage supply; it cannot be connected directly to 5 V.

Design status: This is a researched draft for the initial component-selection submission. Prices are single-unit indicative prices and should be checked before ordering. The microphone choice is provisional until the schematic, PCB assembly method, and 3.3 V supply are confirmed. The power-source model has not yet been selected.

docs.title: 1. Microphone selection
docs.text:
Microphone / Acoustic Sensing

Table 1: Component selection comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1 — 3S 3SM121MZB1UA.Analog MEMS, 6-pin LGA; approximately $1.16 each (previous DigiKey quote).DigiKey product.Datasheet. 66 dBA SNR• low 80 µA typical supply current• single-ended analog output simplifies signal conditioning• larger body than Option 2. 1.6–3.6 V supply not compatible with direct 5 V• bottom acoustic port requires PCB opening and land-pattern care• LGA package is difficult to hand solder• additional regulated supply required. Option 2 — 3S 3SM122KZB1VD-002-R.Analog MEMS, 4-pin LGA; approximately $1.06 each (previous DigiKey quote).DigiKey product. Very small 2.75 × 1.85 mm footprint• 80 µA typical supply current• simple single-ended analog output• omnidirectional detection. Lower 64 dBA SNR• 1.6–3.6 V supply requires a lower-voltage rail• especially small bottom-port LGA is hard to assemble manually• sensitive to acoustic-port contamination. Option 3 — Syntiant SPH11C3LR5H-1.Differential analog MEMS, 5-pin LGA; approximately $2.12 each (previous DigiKey quote).DigiKey product. Best normal-mode SNR of the three (68.5 dBA)• differential output improves noise rejection over longer traces• wide audio frequency response• high acoustic overload tolerance. Higher current (~200–205 µA in normal mode)• differential output complicates interfacing with the current single-ended amplifier design• 2.4–3.2 V normal-mode supply• bottom-port LGA requires careful assembly.

Choice (provisional): Option 1 — 3SM121MZB1UA.

Rationale: Option 1 balances low supply current and noise performance while retaining a single-ended analog output that can be conditioned by the MCP6004 and sampled by RA0. Compared with Option 2 it provides 2 dB better SNR for the same typical current, and it avoids the differential-output interface complexity of Option 3. It is not a drop-in part for the present 5 V rail: a suitable regulated 3.3 V microphone supply and correct bias/coupling network must be designed. The bottom-port LGA footprint and soldering process must also be confirmed before purchase.

Key electrical comparison:

Characteristic Option 1 Option 2 Option 3 (normal mode) Supply voltage 1.6–3.6 V 1.6–3.6 V 2.4–3.2 V Typical current 80 µA 80 µA 200–205 µA Signal-to-noise ratio 66 dBA 64 dBA 68.5 dBA Sensitivity −38 dBV/Pa −38 dBV/Pa −38 dBV/Pa Output Single-ended Single-ended Differential Dimensions 3.76 × 3.00 × 1.10 mm 2.75 × 1.85 × 0.90 mm 3.50 × 2.65 × 1.00 mm

Datasheet evidence: Option 1, page 4; Option 2, page 4; Option 3, pages 2 and 6. The Syntiant microphone's 5 V absolute maximum rating is not its recommended operating voltage.

docs.title: 2. Operational amplifier / signal conditioning
docs.text:
Operational Amplifier / Signal Conditioning

Table 2: Component selection comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1 — Microchip MCP6004-I/P.Quad rail-to-rail op-amp, 14-PDIP; \(0.59–\)0.60 each.DigiKey product. Operates from 1.8–6 V, compatible with the 5 V rail• rail-to-rail input/output• four amplifier channels• low ~100 µA typical supply current per channel• matches existing block diagram. Four channels may be unnecessary• 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product limits very-high-frequency applications• 14-pin DIP uses more PCB area than small surface-mount options. Option 2 — Microchip MCP6002-I/P.Dual rail-to-rail op-amp, 8-PDIP; \(0.44–\)0.45 each.DigiKey product. Same 1.8–6 V supply range• rail-to-rail output• smaller and less expensive if only one or two gain stages are required• low power consumption. Only two channels, limiting later filter/amplifier expansion• requires schematic/pinout changes from MCP6004• 1 MHz bandwidth is not suited to high-frequency amplification. Option 3 — Texas Instruments LM324AN.Quad general-purpose op-amp, 14-PDIP; $0.57 each.DigiKey product. Four channels• inexpensive• familiar and widely used architecture• operates from a single supply. Output is not rail-to-rail, reducing signal swing at 5 V• higher input bias current than MCP6004• less suitable for signals approaching the positive supply rail.

Choice: Option 1 — MCP6004 (package to be finalized for the PCB).

Rationale: The MCP6004 already appears in the individual block diagram and supports operation from the 5 V rail. Its rail-to-rail capability and low current consumption are attractive for conditioning a small microphone signal before the PIC ADC. Four channels leave room for additional gain and filtering stages. The through-hole MCP6004-I/P listed above is a comparison reference; choose the final footprint/package to match the actual PCB manufacturing plan.

Photo note: Images for op-amp options 2 and 3 are representative package photographs; verify the manufacturer marking against the linked product before purchasing.

docs.title: 3. Power regulation
docs.text:
5 V Voltage Regulator

The individual block diagram specifies a 9 V, 3 A unregulated source and 5 V, 1.5 A regulator. The chosen microphone also requires a separate voltage below 3.6 V. The project instructions call for a linear regulator; the following table compares 5 V regulator choices, and a separate 3.3 V candidate is noted below.

Table 3: Component selection comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1 — STMicroelectronics L7805CV.5 V linear regulator, TO-220, nominal 1.5 A; about $1.08 each (verify current price).DigiKey product. Meets the 5 V / 1.5 A nominal target• straightforward linear regulator design• through-hole package is easy to prototype• built-in thermal protection. At 9 V input, heat loss is (9−5) × load current• 6 W dissipation at 1.5 A would require thermal design• does not directly provide the microphone's 3.3 V. Option 2 — Traco Power TSR 1-2450.5 V switching regulator, 1 A maximum; $6.28 each (DigiKey screenshot, October 2026).DigiKey product. Much lower heat dissipation than a linear regulator• wide 6.5–36 V input range• convenient 3-pin SIP replacement form factor. Only 1 A, below the 1.5 A block-diagram specification• higher unit cost• switching noise may need filtering for sensitive analog audio.

Choice (provisional): Option 1 — L7805CV.

Rationale: It meets the stated nominal 5 V, 1.5 A target and provides a simple linear solution. The 1.5 A rating does not mean 1.5 A is available without thermal design. At a full 1.5 A load from 9 V, estimated dissipation would be 6 W, requiring substantial heat management. The actual microphone-board current is expected to be far lower, but must be calculated from final components.

Additional microphone rail: An STMicroelectronics LD1117V33 3.3 V linear regulator (800 mA nominal, DigiKey product, approximately $1.27) is a possible way to provide the lower-voltage microphone supply. Do not finalize this part until the power architecture and regulator input/output capacitor requirements are checked. A 3.3 V rail works for Options 1 and 2, but exceeds Option 3's 3.2 V normal-mode maximum.

Photo note: DigiKey displays a representative TSR-series photo marked TSR 1-2412 on its TSR 1-2450 product listing. The photo represents the package only; the linked product and specified 5 V output are the actual comparison item. Option 1 also uses a representative TO-220 package photograph.

docs.title: 4. Interface and power considerations
docs.text:
• Signal path: Analog MEMS microphone → MCP6004 conditioning → PIC18F57Q43 RA0 (ADC1).
  • Microphone power: 3.3 V for the provisional 3S microphone, not 5 V.
  • Amplifier power: 5 V nominal, subject to final schematic verification.
  • Power budget: Include the PIC, microphone, op-amp, regulator quiescent currents, and any other powered devices actually on this subsystem; include a 25% current margin per rail.
  • Manufacturing: Bottom-port microphones require a PCB acoustic opening and footprint based on the manufacturer's land pattern. Confirm the class PCB process supports these small LGA parts.
  • Design conflict to resolve: Product requirements specify rechargeable power and charging during operation, whereas the block diagram currently shows an unregulated 9 V supply.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: The provisional microphone choice is 3SM121MZB1UA for its 66 dBA SNR, 80 µA typical current, and straightforward single-ended output. The MCP6004 is the preferred amplifier because it supports 5 V operation and is already included in the individual block diagram. A L7805CV is a preliminary 5 V regulator candidate, but the final design must address regulator heating and add a compatible low-voltage microphone rail. Final PCB footprint confirmation and the 3.3 V microphone rail remain open engineering decisions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic represents the microphone subsystem designed for the EGR 304 team project at Arizona State University.

The subsystem includes: - A 5V regulated power supply with fuse protection. - A microphone and MCP6004 operational amplifier for sound detection. - A PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller. - An LED and pushbutton for testing and debugging. - UART TX/RX connections for communication with the main controller. - An ADC input for monitoring the microphone signal.
